_note: Original text written for INTUITY to the Cambridge B2 First Part 5 specification (about 590 words, six questions in text order: detail, inference, reference, purpose, meaning of a phrase and a final question linking the ending to the opening). Each card is a chunk of the article with the question it answers; `highlight` is the sentence that proves the answer, `why` explains the distractors. Used by the Part 5 practice page.
title: Pick a card
subtitle: At seventeen, Kofi Mensah draws crowds of a hundred people with nothing but a pack of cards and a folding table. Jess Harper watched him work.

cards.text: The first trick Kofi Mensah ever performed in public went badly wrong. He was fourteen, standing outside a supermarket in Bristol with a borrowed folding table, and he dropped the entire pack of cards in a puddle. A small boy laughed so hard that he had to sit down. 'That was my whole audience,' Kofi says, 'and honestly, he had a great time.' Three years later, Kofi performs every Saturday on the busiest square in the city, and crowds of a hundred or more are not unusual. He still keeps one of the muddy cards in his wallet.
cards.question: How does Kofi feel now about his first performance?
choices: He is still embarrassed when he remembers it.
He can see the funny side of it.
He thinks the boy was laughing at him unkindly.
He wishes he had practised more beforehand.
cards.highlight: honestly, he had a great time
cards.why: He jokes that his only audience member 'had a great time', which shows he finds it funny now, not embarrassing. Nothing suggests the boy was unkind.

cards.text: He learned his first tricks from online videos, practising in front of the bathroom mirror for hours at a time. His mother, a nurse who worked night shifts, would come home at seven in the morning to find him still awake, shuffling. She tried confiscating the cards. He bought more. She tried hiding them. He found them. 'In the end,' she tells me, 'I made a deal with him. Homework first, then magic. I thought he'd give up within a month.' She pauses. 'His marks actually went up. I've never quite forgiven him for that.'
cards.question: What does Kofi's mother suggest in her final comment?
choices: She is still angry that he ignored her rules.
She thinks magic matters more than schoolwork.
She is disappointed that his marks did not improve more.
She is joking about having been proved wrong.
cards.highlight: I've never quite forgiven him for that.
cards.why: She expected him to 'give up within a month', but his marks 'actually went up', so 'never quite forgiven' is a joke. She is not really angry: the deal worked.

cards.text: What makes Kofi unusual, according to other street performers, is not his skill with cards, impressive though it is. It is the way he talks to people. Most magicians, he explains, treat the audience as people to be fooled. He prefers to treat them as partners in crime. He picks a helper from the crowd, usually the most nervous-looking person he can find, and makes them the hero of the trick. 'They should leave feeling clever, not stupid,' he says. 'If they go home and tell their friends about it, that's my best advertising.'
cards.question: What does 'it' refer to in 'impressive though it is'?
choices: Kofi's skill with cards
the way Kofi talks to people
the opinion of other street performers
the trick he does with a helper
cards.highlight: not his skill with cards, impressive though it is
cards.why: 'It' points back to 'his skill with cards', which is impressive but not what makes him unusual. The way he talks is mentioned only in the next sentence.

cards.text: Street performing has its own rules, and Kofi has learned most of them the hard way. You need a licence from the council. You must not block the entrance to shops. And you must never, ever set up next to a man with bagpipes. On the afternoon I watch him, a sudden shower empties the square in seconds. Kofi simply moves under the shelter of a bus stop and carries on with the four people who have followed him. By the time the sun comes out again, the four have become forty. 'Rain is the best warm-up act,' he grins.
cards.question: Why does the writer describe the rain shower?
choices: to explain why street performers need a licence
to suggest that Kofi's audiences are often very small
to show how Kofi turns a problem to his advantage
to show that Kofi would rather perform indoors
cards.highlight: By the time the sun comes out again, the four have become forty.
cards.why: The rain empties the square, but 'the four have become forty' and he calls rain 'the best warm-up act'. The small crowd is only temporary, so it is not typical.

cards.text: Money is a delicate subject. Kofi does not pass a hat round; instead he leaves an open case at the front and never mentions it. On a good Saturday he can make more than his friends earn in a week of part-time work, but in February he once went home with three pounds and a bus ticket. He insists that is not the point. He is saving for a drama course, and street performing, he says, is the best school there is. 'In a theatre the audience has paid, so they stay. On the street they can walk away whenever they like. That keeps you on your toes.'
cards.question: What does Kofi mean by 'That keeps you on your toes'?
choices: It makes you stay alert and work hard.
It makes you physically tired by the evening.
It forces you to keep moving around the square.
It makes you anxious about earning enough money.
cards.highlight: On the street they can walk away whenever they like. That keeps you on your toes.
cards.why: Because people 'can walk away whenever they like', he must keep their attention. He says money 'is not the point', so it is not about financial worry.

cards.text: At the end of the show, as the crowd drifts away, a small girl comes up and asks how the last trick worked. Kofi kneels down, looks around as if checking for spies, and whispers that a magician can never tell. Then he reaches into his wallet, takes out a slightly muddy four of hearts, and gives it to her. I ask him afterwards whether he minds losing it. He thinks for a moment. 'Not really,' he says. 'A kid laughed at me once and I kept going. Seemed about time to pass it on.'
cards.question: Why does Kofi give the girl the muddy card?
choices: He no longer wants to be reminded of his first show.
He wants to stop her asking about his secrets.
He hopes she will laugh at his mistakes too.
He feels ready to share something that has helped him since he began.
cards.highlight: Seemed about time to pass it on.
cards.why: The card is from the puddle in the opening paragraph, and he says it 'seemed about time to pass it on'. He had already refused to reveal the trick, so the card is not to stop her questions.
